## Abstract

Converting agricultural waste into high-value energy materials is key to sustainable development. Herein, a synergistic carbonization-activation method was used to fabricate hierarchical porous carbon (HPC) embedded with carbon dots (CDs) from walnut shells, addressing low surface activity in conventional biomass-derived carbons. With an optimized KOH-to-carbon ratio (2:1), the resulting PC-2 has a 3D porous network, with CDs anchored on pore walls. It exhibits a maximum specific capacitance of 389 F g^{−1} at 2 mV s^{−1}, which is benefited from CDs-facilitated fast electron transfer and hierarchical pores-enabled efficient ion diffusion. Assembled into a symmetrical supercapacitor, PC-2 delivers 18.6 Wh kg^{−1} at 23.3 W kg^{−1} and 106% performance retention after 5000 cycles. This scalable, eco-friendly route offers insights for designing CDs-integrated structures for next-generation energy storage.

Abstract

Supercapacitors are widely recognized as energy storage solutions due to their high power densities and long cycle lives. Furthermore, there is growing scientific and technological interest in converting biomass waste into carbon materials for manufacturing supercapacitor electrodes. In addition to their abundance and cost-effectiveness, the appeal of carbons derived from biomass lies in their tunable porosity, which enables the rational design of carbon materials to achieve the desired performance of supercapacitors. Here, we present the synthesis of activated carbons from cashew nut shells via potassium hydroxide (KOH) activation at different temperatures (650, 750, and 850 °C). The resulting materials exhibited amorphous and predominant microporous structures. Increasing the activation temperature led to a rise in specific surface area from 1534 to 2034 m^{2}g^{−1}and an increased proportion of mesopores. The electrochemical properties of these activated carbons for supercapacitor applications were investigated by cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge–discharge, and impedance spectroscopic techniques in a 1 M sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) electrolyte. Using a three-electrode system, the activated carbons treated at 750 °C exhibited a maximum specific capacitance of 106 F g^{−1}at a current density of 0.5 A g^{−1}with a good rate capability; they retained 75 % at 10 A g^{−1}over a 1.0 V voltage window. Furthermore, a symmetric supercapacitor coin-cell, fabricated with activated carbons treated at 750 °C as the positive and negative electrodes, demonstrated an energy density of 2.43 Wh kg^{−1}at a power density of 1002 W kg^{−1}. The cell exhibited 87 % capacitance retention at 1.0 A g^{−1}after 10,000 cycles. This work showcases the efficient and sustainable utilization of cashew nut shells as a carbon source for supercapacitor applications and highlights their value in a circular economy.

## 2. Experimental

### 2.1. Materials

CNF (diameter: 5–100 nm) prepared from the mechanical exfoliation of bleached hardwood pulp was supplied by Jinan Shengquan Group Share Holding Co., Ltd. Pre-hydrolysis lignin (PHL, Purity: 92%, M_{w}: 2880 mol g^{-1}) was procured from Shandong Sun Paper Co., Ltd. Hydrochloric acid (HCl), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 98%), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, >99%), and acetylene black were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Nickel foam (ϕ0.4 mm, 0.5 mm) was purchased from Saibo Electrochemical Materials Network.

### 2.2. Preparation of the Lignin-KOH-CNF carbon precursors

Lignin-KOH-CNF carbon precursors with varying CNF and KOH contents were synthesized by simply mixing the lignin, KOH, and CNF in water. Initially, 1.0 g of PHL and various amounts of KOH were sequentially dissolved in 10 mL of deionized water to prepare the carbon precursor solutions. Then, 0.1 g of freeze-dried CNF was added to the mixture at room temperature, followed by ultrasonic treatment for 30 min to ensure uniform dispersion of CNF in the carbon precursor solutions. ## 3. Results and discussion

### 3.1. Characterization of the Lignin, CNF, LK_{x}C_{y}, and CLK_{x}C_{y}

The chemical structures and functional groups of the PHL were confirmed by FTIR, ^{31}P NMR and 2D-HSQC NMR spectroscopy. The FTIR spectrum of the PHL (Fig. S1) exhibited characteristic lignin bands, including O–H stretching at 3455 cm^{-1}, CH_{3} stretching at 2939 cm^{-1}, CH_{2} bending at 2842 cm^{-1}, C=O stretching at 1701 cm^{-1}, and aromatic ring skeletal vibrations at 1604 cm^{-1}, 1508 cm^{-1}, and 1423 cm^{-1}. In addition, the absorption bond at 1457 cm^{-1} corresponded to the C–H vibration of the aromatic ring, while the bond at 1315 cm^{-1} was attributed to syringyl units and condensed guaiacyl groups [18]. The ^{31}P NMR spectra of the PHL was illustrated in Fig. S2, and the corresponding functional group contents were summarized in Table S2. As shown, signals between 146 and 149 ppm were assigned to the aliphatic OH (1.402 mmol g^{-1}). ## 4. Conclusions

A biomass templating strategy was developed by utilizing hydrolysate lignin as the carbon source, CNF as templates, and KOH as an activator, to prepare biomass-derived hierarchical porous carbon materials. The results highlighted that the synergistic effect of CNF templating and KOH activation significantly tailors the pore structure, surface properties, and electrochemical performance of the prepared carbon materials. In detail, the CNF templating induced mesopore formation (≈20 nm diameter), while KOH activation predominantly created micropores and some smaller mesopores (≈4 nm). Benefiting from the high specific surface area (1316.7 m^{2} g^{-1}), large pore volume (0.935 cm^{3} g^{-1}), and well-balanced hierarchical porous structure, the optimized CLK_{100}C_{10} electrode exhibited an outstanding specific capacitance (228.6 F g^{-1} at 0.5 A g^{-1}) and excellent rate capability (maintaining 68.1% of its capacitance at 20 A g^{-1}) in a 6 M KOH electrolyte. Furthermore, the assembled symmetric supercapacitor delivered an energy density of 9.68 Wh·kg^{-1} at a power density of 300 W·kg^{-1}, and exhibited cycling stability with 93.3% capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles. This work provides an effective route for designing high-performance biomass-derived HPC for energy storage applications.
